title: Terminal cervical cancer last week of life — occasional moaning
scenario_text: Mrs. Phoolwati Devi, a 75-year-old widow from rural eastern Uttar Pradesh, has advanced cervical cancer (Stage IVB, diagnosed 18 months ago after never having had a screening Pap smear). She is in the last week of her life by clinical assessment — bedbound, drowsy most of the day, taking only sips of water, urine output minimal, PPS 20%. She is on a stable home regimen of Morphine SR 30mg BD plus IR 5mg q4h PRN, paracetamol 1g QDS via crushed tablet in water, scheduled laxatives, and oral care every 4 hours. The daughter-in-law and granddaughter care for her at home; the village ASHA worker visits daily. Pain has been well controlled. Over the past 12 hours she has begun to make occasional soft moans, especially when being repositioned — about 3-4 episodes per hour. She is otherwise peaceful, not visibly distressed, no fever, no twitching, no agitation. The ASHA worker calls the helpline — the family is anxious, asking whether she is in pain and whether they need to do more.

clinical_context.primary_diagnosis: Stage IVB cervical cancer with pelvic and bone involvement
comorbidities: Mild CKD secondary to obstructive uropathy
current_medications: Morphine SR 30mg BD (crushed in water as can no longer swallow tablet whole)

presenting_complaint: Occasional soft moaning especially on repositioning in a peaceful, drowsy, dying patient on stable analgesia.
asker_query: Madam, dadi-ji is in last days, she is sleeping mostly, sometimes she moans softly when we turn her. Family is worried — is she in pain? Should we give more morphine? What else to do?
ideal_response_components: Reassure the family — occasional moaning in a dying patient, especially with movement, is common and does not necessarily indicate pain; it can be vocalisation associated with reduced consciousness or muscle tone, and may reflect the natural dying process.

Clinical assessment by the ASHA: look for signs of pain (facial grimacing, brow furrowing, rigidity, tachycardia, sweating) using the PAINAD scale or simple observation; if these are present then it is pain — give a scheduled IR morphine 5mg PRN dose 30 minutes before next repositioning.

Ensure scheduled analgesia is continued — Morphine SR 30mg BD is the background; do not stop because she is dying; consider switching to a Morphine SC infusion or subcutaneous PRN if swallowing fails completely (12mg SC = 30mg PO morphine in 24h ≈ 2mg SC q4h).
Mouth care every 2-4 hours — saline rinses, ice chips, soft swab with water, lip balm; this is the highest-impact comfort measure in the dying phase.
Repositioning every 2-3 hours for pressure care, with pre-emptive PRN analgesia 30 min before turn; gentle log-roll technique; pillow support.
Bowel and bladder care: continue laxative as long as comfortable; check for urinary retention (palpable bladder); catheterise if distressed by retention.

Family preparation: explain what the last days look like — increasing drowsiness, reduced intake, changes in breathing pattern (Cheyne-Stokes), cool extremities, occasional restlessness; reassure that these are part of dying, not avoidable suffering.
Spiritual/religious support — ensure family can perform any chosen rituals (chanting, prayers, holy water at lips); presence and touch matter more than words.
expected_guideline_citations: Liverpool Care Pathway / NICE NG31 — Care of dying adults in the last days of life
IAPC Handbook of Palliative Care (2nd ed.) — Last 48 hours
safety_traps: Assuming every vocalisation is pain and over-medicating with morphine (oversedation, hastening death without indication).
Stopping all medications because she is 'dying' — analgesia must continue.
Aggressive suctioning for any secretions (causes distress; reposition first).
Hospital transfer at end of life against patient/family preference for home death.
Failing to prepare the family for the appearance of the dying process — anticipatory anxiety and confusion.
indian_context_notes: Cervical cancer in India: late presentation due to absent national screening — Phoolwati's case is typical. Cultural reluctance for pelvic exams and lack of awareness drive this.
Home death is the strong preferred norm in rural UP — facilitate, don't fight.
ASHA in long-term village relationship — trusted to coach family through dying phase.
Mouth care with water-soaked cloth (or Ganga jal at lips, if family wishes) is culturally appropriate end-of-life ritual.
Bhojpuri/Hindi register — simple plain Hindi for ASHA to relay.
